meta.title: Who really said "If you can't convince them, confuse them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Truman really said it — in 1948, as an accusation. He called it "an old political trick." The adage was in print by 1919; quote books dropped the context.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you can't convince them, confuse them'?
meta.ogDescription: Truman said the words twice in 1948 — both times attacking opponents for using the trick. The adage predates him. Primary sources and the citation trail.

answer.label: Not Truman's maxim — he was quoting a trick he condemned
answer.sourceLine: Truman really did say these words — twice in the 1948 campaign — but never as advice. At Dexter, Iowa on 18 September 1948 he called it “an old political trick”; at Raleigh, North Carolina on 19 October 1948 he called it “the old Republican doctrine.” Both times he was accusing his opponents of using it. Quote Investigator finds the adage already in print in 1919, and treats Truman as the man who popularised it rather than the man who coined it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Harry S. Truman, quoting an adage he pinned on his opponents
Address at Dexter, Iowa, on the Occasion of the National Plowing Match

source.excerpt: On the one hand, the Republicans are telling industrial workers that the high cost of food in the cities is due to this Government’s farm policy. On the other hand, the Republicans are telling the farmers that the high cost of manufactured goods on the farm is due to this Government’s labor policy. That’s plain hokum. It’s an old political trick. “If you can’t convince ’em, confuse ’em.” But this time it won’t work.
trail: The Truman Library’s public papers text of the Dexter address ↗ carries the line in full: “That’s plain hokum. It’s an old political trick. ‘If you can’t convince ’em, confuse ’em.’ But this time it won’t work.” The scare quotes are in the official text.

A month into the campaign, Truman used the familiar wording himself. The American Presidency Project’s text of his address at the State Fairgrounds, Raleigh, North Carolina, 19 October 1948 ↗ reads: “I don’t think you are going to be the victims this time of the old Republican doctrine: ‘If you can’t convince them, confuse them.’”

Quote Investigator ↗ traces the maxim back well before Truman: its earliest located use in print is an article by A. C. Wilson in the Manchester Quarterly in 1919, describing the character Christopher Vance in a William De Morgan novel — “If you cannot convince them, confuse them” might have been his motto. QI notes Wilson may himself have been repeating an existing adage.

Barry Popik’s citation file ↗ shows how quickly it detached from Truman: the Richmond Times-Dispatch of 19 September 1948 reported the Dexter line with “them” for “’em,” and by 21 December 1950 a letter in the Pittsburgh Press was already calling it “the old adage.”
source.cutTag: He was the prosecutor, not the author
source.excerptNote: At Dexter, Truman used the clipped “’em” form. The exact wording that circulates today appears in his address at the State Fairgrounds in Raleigh, North Carolina on 19 October 1948: “I don’t think you are going to be the victims this time of the old Republican doctrine: ‘If you can’t convince them, confuse them.’” In both speeches the quotation marks are Truman’s own — he was citing somebody else’s maxim.

author.name: Harry S. Truman
author.heading: About Harry S. Truman
author.bio: Truman succeeded to the presidency on Franklin Roosevelt’s death in 1945 and won a term of his own in the 1948 election, campaigning in a punishing whistle-stop tour that most observers expected him to lose. The Dexter and Raleigh speeches belong to that campaign, and both show his characteristic method: name the opponent’s tactic out loud, in the opponent’s own words, and let the audience judge it. It is a rhetorical habit that has cost him repeatedly in the quotation books — the maxims he held up for scorn read, stripped of their setting, like maxims he endorsed.

misattribution.heading: How Truman got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote — it is a real one with its meaning turned inside out. Truman spoke the words, but every time he did, he put them in quotation marks and handed them to his opponents. Strip the sentence out of the paragraph and the accuser becomes the adviser.

items.why: Truman introduced the line as “an old political trick” at Dexter and as “the old Republican doctrine” at Raleigh — he was naming a tactic, not coining one. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the adage “was in circulation by 1919” and that Truman “helped to popularize the expression… but he was not endorsing the approach outlined by the maxim. He was criticizing it.”

Quote Investigator records that Peter’s 1977 Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time printed it as “Truman’s Law — If you can’t convince them, confuse them” credited to Truman, without providing any context ↗. Paul Dickson’s The Official Rules carries the same “Truman’s Law” heading, as Barry Popik documents ↗. That is the form most quote sites still reprint.

A “Show Time” column in the Richmond Times-Dispatch of 20 July 1964 offered it as “Will Rogers’ advice: ‘If you can’t convince ’em, confuse ’em’” — recorded in Popik’s citation file ↗. No source ties the line to Rogers; it is the sort of drift a widely circulating proverb attracts.

misattribution.truthLine: Truman said it, twice, in the autumn of 1948 — both times as an accusation against his opponents. Wikiquote flags the problem directly: his mention of an “old political trick” is often quoted alone as if it were a strategy he was advising rather than one he was criticizing ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Dexter speech was an attack on a specific piece of two-faced messaging. Truman told the crowd that Republicans were blaming urban food prices on the administration’s farm policy while simultaneously blaming farm costs on its labour policy — a story tuned to whichever audience was listening. “That’s plain hokum,” he said, and then named the technique.

So the line was never a wink at the reader. It was an indictment, delivered with the maxim held up like an exhibit. That is precisely what makes it such an efficient misquote: the sentence is quotable on its own, sounds like worldly advice, and carries a president’s name — and the paragraph that reverses it does not fit on a poster.
detailsBody: At Dexter Truman used the spoken contraction — “If you can’t convince ’em, confuse ’em” — and the next day’s Richmond Times-Dispatch printed it as “them.” A month later at Raleigh, Truman used “them” himself. Both forms are authentically his; neither is his invention.

The 1919 attestation Quote Investigator found is not a political one at all. A. C. Wilson was writing in the Manchester Quarterly about Christopher Vance, a character in a William De Morgan novel who baffled people to get his way — the maxim was offered as what might have been his motto. Whether Wilson coined it or was repeating something already current, QI does not settle.

schema.verdictNote: Truman spoke both wordings in the 1948 campaign — “If you can’t convince ’em, confuse ’em” at Dexter, Iowa on 18 September and “If you can’t convince them, confuse them” at Raleigh, North Carolina on 19 October — but each time he quoted the maxim as his opponents’ tactic, calling it an old political trick and the old Republican doctrine. He popularised the saying; he did not coin it. The adage was already in print in 1919.

sourcesVerified.claim: Truman's Dexter, Iowa address of 18 September 1948 contains verbatim: "That's plain hokum. It's an old political trick. 'If you can't convince 'em, confuse 'em.' But this time it won't work." — preceded by the passage about Republicans telling workers and farmers contradictory stories.

Truman's address at the State Fairgrounds, Raleigh, North Carolina, dated 19 October 1948, contains: "I don't think you are going to be the victims this time of the old Republican doctrine:" / "If you can't convince them, confuse them." / "I think you know who your real friends are and who your enemies are."

Quote Investigator concludes: "the adage was in circulation by 1919. Currently, the earliest use in print was from the pen of A. C. Wilson. Harry Truman helped to popularize the expression when he used it in a speech in 1948, but he was not endorsing the approach outlined by the maxim. He was criticizing it." QI identifies the 1919 item as A. C. Wilson's Manchester Quarterly article on the character Christopher Vance in a William De Morgan novel, wording "If you cannot convince them, confuse them," and notes Wilson may have been presenting a pre-existing adage. QI also records Laurence J. Peter's 1977 Peter's Quotations printing "Truman's Law — If you can't convince them, confuse them. —Harry S Truman" without context.

Barry Popik's page documents: the Richmond Times-Dispatch of 19 September 1948 reporting the Dexter line as "If you can't convince them, confuse them"; the Evening World-Herald of 19 October 1948 carrying Truman's "old Republican doctrine" line; a 21 December 1950 Pittsburgh Press letter calling it "the old adage"; a 20 July 1964 Richmond Times-Dispatch column crediting "Will Rogers' advice: 'If you can't convince 'em, confuse 'em'"; and Paul Dickson's The Official Rules listing it as "Truman's Law" credited to Harry S Truman.

Wikiquote's Harry S. Truman page carries the Dexter passage sourced to the Address at the National Plowing Match (18 September 1948), as quoted in Miracle of '48 (2003), ed. Steve Neal, together with the editorial note: "Truman's mention of an 'old political trick' is often quoted alone as if it were a strategy he was advising rather than one he was criticizing."
